# Follow Thy Fair Sun, Unhappy Shadow

Follow thy fair sun, unhappy shadow,
Though thou be black as night
And she made all of light,
Yet follow thy fair sun unhappy shadow.

Follow her whose light thy light depriveth,
Though here thou liv'st disgraced,
And she in heaven is placed,
Yet follow her whose light the world reviveth.

Follow those pure beams whose beauty burneth,
That so have scorched thee,
As thou still black must be,
Till her kind beams thy black to brightness turneth.

Follow her while yet her glory shineth,
There comes a luckless night,
That will dim all her light,
And this the black unhappy shade divineth.

Follow still, since so thy fates ordained,
The Sun must have his shade,
Till both at once do fade,
The Sun still proved, the shadow still disdained.

---

*Poetry Out Loud Note: In the printed anthology, this poem appears under the title "Follow Thy Fair Sun, Unhappy Shadow." Students may recite either the formal title or the poem's opening line, as both are considered acceptable.*

outputs.L3:
# The Faithful Shadow

The poem opens with a striking command: an "unhappy shadow" must follow its "fair sun," though the two exist in complete and irreconcilable contrast. One is black as the depths of night; the other is a being composed wholly of light. This paradox forms the emotional core of the verse—a devotion that persists not because of compatibility, but in spite of its absence. The shadow's very nature seems to disqualify it from proximity to such radiance, yet the command to follow remains unwavering.

This asymmetry deepens when we consider the shadow's earthly station. While the shadow lives in disgrace, bound to the humble ground, the one it follows—luminous and exalted—is enthroned in heaven itself. This is no arbitrary hierarchy; it is justified by function and worth: her light revives the world. She sustains and nourishes existence itself, while the shadow can offer only its dark, silent pursuit. The disparity in their positions mirrors the disparity in their purposes—one gives life, the other merely trails behind.

Yet the shadow's darkness is not incidental—it is a direct consequence of the sun's own power. The poem reveals that the sun's pure, burning beams are precisely what scorched the shadow black in the first place. The very source of the shadow's suffering is also, paradoxically, its only hope of redemption: those same kind beams possess the power to eventually transform that darkness into brightness. Thus, the shadow's affliction and its salvation both originate from the same radiant source, binding it inescapably to the very being that wounded it.

A somber prescience runs through the poem as well. The shadow senses, with quiet foreboding, that a "luckless night" will someday arrive to dim the sun's glory—for even the most brilliant light is not immune to eclipse or ending. And yet, this knowledge changes nothing: the shadow must still follow while her light currently shines, embracing devotion in the present rather than being paralyzed by the inevitability of future loss.

The poem closes with a meditation on fate itself. It has been ordained that the sun must always have its shadow, the two locked in an eternal, inseparable pairing until they fade together into whatever end awaits them. Yet even this shared destiny is not one of equality: the sun will ultimately be proved worthy, vindicated and celebrated, while the shadow remains disdained—loyal to the end, yet never granted the honor it so faithfully served.
outputs.L4:
# The Shadow and the Sun

In the quiet spaces between light and darkness, there exists a shadow condemned to an eternal pursuit—forever chasing a sun it can never touch, never possess, never truly know. This is the central image around which the poem builds its melancholy architecture: a dark form perpetually trailing behind brilliance, bound by an invisible thread of longing to a celestial body that burns too bright, too distant, too indifferent to notice the faithful darkness that follows in its wake.

The poem uses this natural phenomenon—the inseparable relationship between light source and shadow—as a profound metaphor for a love that exists in painful imbalance. One figure, cast as the shadow, represents the lover who gives everything: constancy, devotion, an unwavering presence that shifts and moves only in response to the beloved's own motion. The other, embodied by the sun, represents the beloved who remains luminous, self-sufficient, and largely unaware of—or indifferent to—the shadow's silent suffering. The sun does not choose to be followed; it simply exists in its radiance, and the shadow has no choice but to trail behind, shaped entirely by a light that offers no warmth in return.

This is love's cruelest architecture: one soul scorned, overshadowed, and diminished by the very brilliance it adores. The shadow cannot help its position—it is not a matter of choice but of nature, of fundamental design. Just as physics dictates that a shadow must follow its light source, so too does the poem suggest that some hearts are simply constructed to pursue what they cannot have, to remain forever secondary, forever in the periphery of another's glow.

Yet the poem does not offer easy resolution or hope for eventual reciprocity. Instead, it presents a stark and somewhat tragic truth: this unequal devotion is fated to continue not until love is returned, not until the shadow is finally seen or valued, but until both shadow and sun fade together into nothingness. Only in mutual extinction—when the light dims and the darkness that depended upon it dissolves in turn—does the chase finally end. There is no triumphant reunion, no moment where the shadow steps into the light and is embraced as an equal. There is only the slow, inevitable fading of both parties, the shadow disappearing precisely because the sun it followed has ceased to shine.

In this way, the poem captures something achingly true about unrequited and unequal love: its persistence despite pain, its refusal to be reasoned away, and its ultimate resolution only through loss rather than fulfillment. The shadow's devotion is both beautiful and heartbreaking—a testament to loyalty that receives no reward, a love that exists purely for its own sake because it has no other choice. The poem leaves us with the poignant image of two entities bound together not by mutual affection, but by an inescapable natural law, destined to move through existence in tandem until the final darkness claims them both, shadow and sun, together and yet never truly united.
outputs.L5:
# Follow, Though, And

There is something quietly profound in these three small words, each carrying weight far beyond its size.

**Follow** speaks to one of humanity's oldest instincts—the desire to trace a path, to trust a direction, to move toward something beyond ourselves. We follow rivers to their source, follow arguments to their conclusions, follow mentors who show us what we might become. To follow is to admit that we do not yet know everything, that someone or something ahead of us holds knowledge worth pursuing. Yet following is not merely submission. The best followers are also seekers—they follow not blindly, but with open eyes, ready to recognize when the path shifts or when it's time to walk alone.

**Though** is the word of nuance, the small hinge on which complexity turns. It refuses simple stories. Whenever we say "though," we admit that reality resists our tidy conclusions. *I love this city, though its winters are long. She was frightened, though she did not show it.* Though is honesty's quiet companion—it prevents us from painting the world in absolutes, reminding us that most truths come with exceptions, most feelings arrive tangled with their opposites. To think in "thoughs" is to think maturely, to hold two truths at once without needing to resolve them into one.

**And** is perhaps the most humble word of all, yet it does the heaviest lifting. It is the word of accumulation, of relationship, of things existing together rather than in isolation. Life rarely delivers single, clean events—it delivers *this and that*, joy and grief, effort and reward, arriving not in sequence but tangled together. And connects sentences, but it also connects lives: your story and mine, the past and the present, what was promised and what came to be. Without "and," nothing could build upon anything else; the world would remain a scattering of isolated facts rather than a woven whole.

Together, these three words tell us something about how we live: we **follow** paths not fully seen, we hold complexity through the word **though**, and we build meaning by connecting everything with **and**. In their smallness, they carry the architecture of thought itself.

# "Follow Your Saint" (also known as "Follow Thy Fair Sun")
### by Thomas Campion

Follow thy fair sun, unhappy shadow,
Though thou be black as night
And she made all of light,
Yet follow thy fair sun, unhappy shadow.

Follow her whose light thy light depriveth,
Though here thou liv'st disgraced,
And she in heaven is placed,
Yet follow her whose light the world reviveth.

Follow those pure beams whose beauty burneth,
That so have scorchèd thee,
As thou still black must be,
Till her kind beams thy black to brightness turneth.

Follow her while yet her glory shineth:
There comes a luckless night,
That will dim all her light;
And this the black unhappy shade divineth.

Follow still since so thy fates ordained;
The sun must have his shade,
Till both at once do fade,
The sun still proved, the shadow still disdained.

---

**Note on the title:** This poem is frequently anthologized under the title **"Follow Your Saint"**, which reflects its placement as the second song in Campion's *A Book of Airs* (1601), where it was paired musically and thematically with the poem "Follow Your Saint, Follow with Accents Sweet." However, many print anthologies—particularly those focused on imagery and thematic content rather than the original song-book context—prefer the title **"Follow Thy Fair Sun"**, drawn directly from the poem's first line, since this title more directly signals the poem's central conceit of light, shadow, and unrequited devotion. The "shadow" (the speaker) addresses itself in the second person, urging perpetual, hopeless pursuit of the "sun" (the beloved), a metaphor for the poet's unequal and painful devotion.
